title: 2 Americans win Nobel Prize in economics for work on boom-bust cycles
summary:

Economics can helpTwo Americans have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on how to smooth boom-and-bust cycles to limit inflation and unemployment.
This award is not one of the original five, but a "memorial" prize that honors Alfred Nobel.

title: It's taking longer to find a new job after losing one
summary:
It's taking longer to find a new job after losing onetoggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images North AmericaEvan Smith lost his job with Trader Interactive this past spring, when the online platform for trading RVs and other vehicles was sold.
The average worker is taking longer to find a new job, and that means more people are exhausting their unemployment benefits before any new paychecks begin.
"When you're one of the people that doesn't have a job, it doesn't really matter what the percentage is," says Cheryl Huff.
Colorado offers six months of unemployment benefits, and Huff's are set to run out in early December.
"My wife, usually on a Friday when we're sitting on the back porch after work — after she gets done with work — she's like, 'How are you feeling?'"

title: 2 American economists win Nobel for work on managing economic shocks
summary:
"The laureates' research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before," the Nobel committee wrote in a paper explaining the economists' work.
"Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,'' the Nobel committee wrote.
Advertisement Advertisement"If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,'' the committee wrote.
Advertisement Advertisement"Unlike the traditional Keynesian models, Woodford's model recommends a cooling measure, such as increased interest rates, to avoid uncontrolled inflation," the Nobel committee wrote.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.

title: 3 charts sum up why many US households are struggling right now
summary:
The S&P 500 (^GSPC) trading near a record high doesn't mean all is fine and dandy in the US economy.
Quite the contrary for many households as they battle higher costs for gas, fuel, and medical insurance this year.
Here are several charts from the Goldman Sachs team that shed light on the realities facing many US households, and why a lot of consumer companies are struggling.
Household debt is on the riseWith the cost of living remaining high, households are taking on more debt to get by.
· Goldman SachsPersonal savings are dwindlingIn addition to taking on more debt, households have dipped into their savings to spend on what they need to spend on.

title: Fed officials are warning of more pain. Many Americans are already feeling it
summary:
Now, with the Fed back to raising interest rates for the first time in three years, a familiar warning about the economic fallout is resurfacing.
When price increases become too rapid, the Fed typically raises interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for consumers and businesses.
And now the Fed comes with a cure: higher interest rates,” Beth Ann Bovino, chief economist at US Bank, said.
For now, though, economic pain isn’t being felt equally.
For the Fed, the challenge is figuring out how much pain the economy can withstand — and which risk is worse: acting too soon or waiting too long.

title: Losing your job after age 50 could derail your career
summary:
Some older workers who lose their jobs can afford to retire, while others find a comparable role fairly quickly.
But those figures obscure a worse trend for older job seekers.

Heep suspects some employers may favor younger job seekers over someone his age because they worry he won't remain in the workforce much longer.
And for older job seekers who suspect their age is holding them back, there's often no clear path to addressing the problem.

title: Two Sigma, the $80 billion quant fund, is raising the bar for interns after a very productive summer
summary:
So productive that it's raising the bar for future interns.
"We put as much into the onboarding and training of our interns as we do our full-time employees," Anger said.
Now, after the successful summer, Two Sigma is rethinking the skills it emphasizes in its internships and what it's looking for in new hires.
AI, Anger said, has raised expectations for the "depth and contribution" an intern can achieve in their few months on the job.
Two Sigma extended full-time offers to 85% of interns who had finished school out of its most recent cohort.
